title: Λύκος καὶ ἵππος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 225. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λύκος κατά τινα ἄρουραν ὁδεύων κριθὰς εὗρε· μὴ δυνάμενος δὲ αὐταῖς τροφῇ χρήσασθαι, καταλιπὼν ἀπῄει.
sentences.tr: Lykos kata tina arouran hodeuōn krithas heure· mē dynamenos de autais trophēi chrēsasthai, katalipōn apēiei.
sentences.l: A wolf, journeying over a certain ploughland, found barley; but not being able to use it as food, he left it behind and was going away.
sentences.n: χράομαι takes the dative of the thing used (αὐταῖς), with a second dative τροφῇ naming what it is used as: 'to use them for food.' ἀπῄει is the imperfect of ἄπειμι, 'was going away' — the departure is still in progress when the horse turns up in the next sentence.

sentences.t: Ἵππῳ δὲ συντυχών, τοῦτον ἐπὶ τὴν ἄρουραν ἐπήγαγε λέγων ὡς εὑρὼν κριθὰς αὐτὸς μὲν οὐκ ἔφαγεν, αὐτῷ δὲ ἐφύλαξεν, ἐπεὶ καὶ ἡδέως αὐτοῦ τὸν ψόφον τῶν ὀδόντων ἀκούει.
sentences.tr: Hippōi de syntychōn, touton epi tēn arouran epēgage legōn hōs heurōn krithas autos men ouk ephagen, autōi de ephylaxen, epei kai hēdeōs autou ton psophon tōn odontōn akouei.
sentences.l: But having fallen in with a horse, he brought him to the ploughland, saying that, having found barley, he himself had not eaten it, but had kept it for him, since he even hears the sound of his teeth with pleasure.
sentences.i: But falling in with a horse, he brought him to the field, saying that he had found barley and had not eaten it himself but had kept it for him, since he took pleasure even in the sound of his teeth.
sentences.n: συντυγχάνω takes the dative of the person met. ὡς after a verb of saying introduces reported speech, and Greek keeps the tenses of the words as first spoken — ἔφαγεν and ἐφύλαξεν stay aorist, ἀκούει stays present, where English shifts them back into the past.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ ἵππος ὑποτυχὼν εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’, ὦ οὗτος, εἰ λύκοι κριθῶν τροφῇ χρῆσθαι ἠδύναντο, οὐκ ἄν ποτε τὰ ὦτα τῆς γαστρὸς προέκρινας. »
sentences.tr: Kai ho hippos hypotychōn eipen· « All’, ō houtos, ei lykoi krithōn trophēi chrēsthai ēdynanto, ouk an pote ta ōta tēs gastros proekrinas. »
sentences.l: And the horse, taking-up-the-word, said: « But, you there, if wolves were able to make use of barley-food, you would never have preferred your ears to your belly. »
sentences.i: And the horse took him up and said: « But, you there — if wolves could make food of barley, you would never have set your ears above your belly. »
sentences.n: ὑποτυχών is the house rendering 'taking-up-the-word': to catch up what has just been said and answer it, not to seize anything physically. κριθῶν is a genitive depending on τροφῇ — 'barley-food' — not a second object of χρῆσθαι as in the first sentence, where αὐταῖς was the thing used and τροφῇ named what it was used as. The condition is contrary to fact, and it mixes tenses on purpose: an imperfect protasis for the standing fact (wolves cannot eat barley) and an aorist apodosis for the single act (you would never have made that choice). προκρίνω takes the accusative of what is preferred and the genitive of what it is preferred to. The ears are the pleasure of listening; the belly is the meal the wolf is not offering.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι οἱ φύσει πονηροί, κἂν χρηστότητα ἐπαγγέλλωνται, οὐ πιστεύονται.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti hoi physei ponēroi, kan chrēstotēta epangellōntai, ou pisteuontai.
sentences.l: The story shows that those who are wicked by nature, even if they profess honesty, are not believed.
sentences.n: φύσει is a dative of respect, 'in their nature.' κἂν is καὶ ἐάν crushed together, 'even if,' and takes the subjunctive (ἐπαγγέλλωνται). ἐπαγγέλλομαι in the middle is to make a profession of something, to advertise oneself as having it. πιστεύω takes a dative in the active, but its passive is made personal all the same: 'they are not believed.'
